name: Joule’s refined heat equivalent
summary: Joule's refined value of about 772 foot-pounds per British thermal unit, from friction in water, mercury and iron, became the working figure used by physicists.
description: Water, mercury and cast-iron friction series compared expended mechanical work with corrected heating. Joule preferred the water result 772.692 foot-pounds and rounded his conclusion to 772 per pound of water warmed by 1 °F near 55–60 °F.
tier_reason: Quantitative equivalence of heat and work supplied thermodynamic reasoning and energy accounting across physics and engineering.

impact.note: The exact value made physicists rebuild heat theory around equivalence, but the platform credit belongs to the wider principle, so it scores below tier 0.

why: Joule's earlier determinations disagreed with one another, and a precise figure was needed before heat–work equivalence could be used in calculation.

market.note: Commercial availability is not a milestone of a scientific knowledge result.

date.label: 1849 report
date.basis: Paper dated 4 June, received 6 June, read 21 June 1849; 1850 is its journal publication year.

events.statement: Water, mercury and cast-iron friction series compared expended mechanical work with corrected heating. Joule preferred the water result 772.692 foot-pounds and rounded his conclusion to 772 per pound of water warmed by 1 °F near 55–60 °F.
events.caveats: Historical result and thermal reference conditions are retained. No claim that the last digits represent modern accuracy; Joule explicitly notes residual vibration and sound.

evidence.locator: Printed p. 61 dates; pp. 69–70 corrections; p. 82 Table IX, qualification and final dated conclusion (visually checked)
evidence.supports: Reported chronology, multiple friction series, preferred numerical result, units and qualifications.

date.label: 1852 publication
date.basis: Thomson’s detailed printed credit or use appears in the Philosophical Magazine volume for July–December 1852. A 1851 reading is not treated as proof of the exact contents of that oral presentation.

events.statement: Thomson cited Joule’s value of approximately 772.69 and used a rounded equivalent in calculations in the 1852 printed paper.
events.scope: Joule’s corrected water-friction result 772.692 foot-pounds per pound of water per Fahrenheit degree.
events.caveats: Thomson refers to a 32–33 °F thermal unit, while Joule’s water experiments were near 55–60 °F. The exact oral contents of the earlier 1851 reading have not been independently established.

evidence.supports: The 1852 original journal printing explicitly contains the stated credit or numerical use.

evidence.locator: Printed p. 82 Table IX and conclusion
evidence.supports: Gives the 772.692 water result and Joule’s rounded conclusion.
